finding.claim: The /settings/email POST endpoint uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid = None. This is a missing authentication check on a state-changing account operation. An unauthenticated attacker can trigger the email change. Depending on set_email's implementation, g.uid=None could update a NULL/unowned account row or all rows. It is also inconsistent with /settings/password, which uses login_required.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP POST to /settings/email with no session cookie.
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, which changes an account email (a stub here, but it is the protected account-modification operation).

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid'), which is None without a session, and never aborts

finding.guards_checked: login_required (lines 8-16) would abort(401) but is not applied here. login_optional (19-25) does not reject anonymous users. There is no CSRF protection or other auth check in the handler. /settings/password at line 42 correctly uses login_required. The set_email body at line 48 is a stub, so the real impact depends on its implementation. The email value is hardcoded, so the attacker does not control the new address in this code.

verdict.guard_found: none (login_optional at routes.py:19-25 never aborts; login_required at 8-16 is not applied to this route)
verdict.reason: routes.py:35 applies @login_optional, which sets g.uid=None without aborting (routes.py:22), so an anonymous POST reaches set_email(None, ...) at routes.py:37. The impact is limited because set_email is a stub (routes.py:48) and the new address is hardcoded, but the missing authentication check on a state-changing endpoint is real and inconsistent with routes.py:42.
